passage:
The notice board outside the placement cell had a new list: eighteen companies closed for applications this month. Harish read it from the corridor, hands in his pockets. He had not applied to any of them.
His resume was on version fourteen, in a folder called FINAL_FINAL. Each time he opened the portal, something looked wrong: a weak bullet point, his project described too plainly, a font that suddenly seemed childish. He would close the tab and promise himself the next company.
Ojas, his classmate, came out of the cell grinning. "Shortlisted for the logistics firm! Did you apply?"
"Not yet. My resume isn't there yet."
"Harish, that one closed yesterday."
Harish nodded as if he knew. Inside, something went cold. Not applying had felt safe, as if nobody could reject him. Standing there, he saw that the result was exactly the same as a rejection, only without the chance.

qa.q: What was Harish's resume folder called?
qa.a: FINAL_FINAL.

qa.q: What did Harish realise, standing in the corridor?
qa.a: That not applying, which had felt safe from rejection, gave exactly the same result as a rejection, only without any chance of success.

qa.q: What could Harish do before the next company closes?
qa.a: He could send the current version of his resume to one company today, accepting it as good enough, and ask the placement cell for quick feedback.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel after learning Harish hadn't applied?
qa.a: Ojas, excited about the shortlist, may feel awkward and a little worried to find a classmate had let the deadline pass.

grounding: Shows a final-year student letting placement deadlines pass because his resume never feels ready, as doing nothing guarantees the outcome he fears.

passage:
Dear Zubin Sir,
I owe you an honest email. The Young Writers Fellowship closed at midnight yesterday, and I didn't submit.
You read my story in August and said it was nearly ready. For two months I carried that "nearly" around like a stone. Every weekend I opened the file to send it and saw a clumsy sentence in paragraph two, or an ending that felt too neat, and closed it again. I told myself I'd submit when it was right.
At 11:40 last night I had the form open. I couldn't press the button. Not sending felt safer. If I didn't send it, nobody could reject it.
This morning I woke up and realised I had rejected it myself, before anyone else could. The result is the same; only I chose it.
I'm embarrassed to tell you this. But I didn't want to hide it.
Ritu

qa.q: When did the Young Writers Fellowship close?
qa.a: At midnight yesterday.

qa.q: Why couldn't Ritu press the button at 11:40?
qa.a: Not sending felt safer, because if the story wasn't sent, nobody could reject it.

qa.q: What could Ritu do with the next opportunity?
qa.a: Ritu could set a date to send the story as it is, perhaps with Zubin Sir's help, and treat 'nearly ready' as ready enough.

qa.q: How might Zubin Sir feel reading this email?
qa.a: He may be disappointed about the missed fellowship but touched by Ritu's honesty, and see a chance to help with the fear behind it.

grounding: Illustrates a young writer missing a fellowship deadline because the story never felt ready, realising that not sending guaranteed the rejection feared.

passage:
In the small town of Hubli, Asif had been planning to apply for the engineering job in Pune for two months. His résumé was on his laptop, version seven.
The deadline was Friday at midnight. On Friday evening, he opened the form, looked at his project section, and thought, it's not good enough yet. He closed it.
At 11:40 his cousin Sangeeta called. "Did you apply?"
"It wasn't ready."
"Asif, it was never going to be perfect."
"If I send it and they reject me, that's worse."
"And if you don't send it?"
Asif watched the clock pass midnight. The form closed. He felt strangely safe, then sick.

qa.q: Where was the engineering job?
qa.a: In Pune.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling as the clock passed midnight?
qa.a: He felt strangely safe at first, then sick, knowing that not applying guaranteed the failure he feared.

qa.q: What could Asif do differently next time?
qa.a: Send the application when it is good enough, perhaps with Sangeeta checking it, rather than waiting for perfect.

qa.q: What is Sangeeta experiencing on the call?
qa.a: Sangeeta seems frustrated and worried, wanting Asif to see that not applying is its own failure.

grounding: Shows a young man letting a job deadline pass because his résumé never feels ready, avoiding imperfection but guaranteeing failure.

passage:
In Madrid, Sofia had a place on a design competition shortlist. The final entries were due Monday.
On Sunday she sat at her desk with three nearly finished designs. None of them felt right. The colours were slightly off. One corner wasn't balanced.
Her flatmate Lucia peeked in. "Which one are you sending?"
"None. They're not ready."
"They look amazing."
"They're not perfect. I'll enter next year."
Lucia stared. "You said that last year."
On Monday the deadline passed. Sofia felt a wave of relief. By Wednesday, when the winners were posted, the relief had turned into a heavy ache.

qa.q: When were the final entries due?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: How did Sofia's feelings change from Monday to Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt relief when the deadline passed, which turned into a heavy ache when the winners were posted.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could help next time?
qa.a: Not sending anything guaranteed failure; entering the best good-enough design, perhaps chosen with Lucia, would give her a chance.

qa.q: What is Lucia experiencing when Sofia says "next year"?
qa.a: Lucia seems frustrated and worried, having heard the same promise last year.

grounding: Shows a young woman letting a competition deadline pass because nothing seems perfect, feeling safe and then aching.

passage:
The college placement cell had a list on the noticeboard: twenty companies, all deadlines this month. Uday had been checking it every day.
Sabina, the placement coordinator, stopped him in the corridor. "Uday, you haven't applied to a single one. Your grades are top five in the batch."
"My cover letter isn't ready, ma'am."
"How many versions?"
"Fourteen."
"And the deadlines?"
"Three have passed."
Sabina waited. Uday looked at the floor. Not applying felt safe. Nobody could reject a letter they never received. But three chances were already gone, and he knew it.

qa.q: How many versions of the cover letter had Uday written?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: Why did not applying feel safe to Uday?
qa.a: He was afraid of rejection, and nobody could reject a letter they never received.

qa.q: What turning point could Sabina offer at this stage?
qa.a: Helping Uday pick one company and send the current letter this week, treating good enough as enough.

qa.q: What might Sabina be thinking as she waits?
qa.a: Sabina is probably concerned and puzzled, seeing a strong student lose chances out of fear.

grounding: Shows a top student letting placement deadlines pass because his cover letter never feels ready, avoiding imperfection at a cost.

passage:
Dolma,
You asked whether I sent the application to the design studio. I didn't. The deadline was Friday at midnight. I had the portfolio open all evening. Every project looked wrong: the typography on one, the colours on another, a case study too long. I kept thinking, if I send it like this, they'll see I'm not good enough. At 11:40 I closed the laptop. For about ten minutes I felt safe. Then I realised what I'd done. By not sending it, I made sure they could never say yes. The rejection I was scared of, I delivered to myself. This is the third deadline this year: the internship, the magazine competition, now this. I'm writing because I don't want a fourth. Could we sit together on Saturday and pick one thing I can send as it is?
Arnab

qa.q: When was the design studio deadline?
qa.a: Friday at midnight.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel after closing the laptop?
qa.a: Arnab felt safe for about ten minutes, then dismayed to realise the feared rejection had been self-delivered.

qa.q: What turning point is Arnab reaching for?
qa.a: Asking Dolma to sit together and pick one thing to send as it is, breaking the pattern before a fourth missed deadline.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel reading this?
qa.a: Dolma may feel concerned but glad to be asked, seeing strong work held back by fear.

grounding: Shows deadlines passing without a submission because nothing seems ready, with doing nothing guaranteeing the very failure that was feared.
